title: Inverse Sampling Transform
text: Throughout this article, we use the following notations:

title: Inverse Sampling Transform
text:
1 Background

Proposition 1 For any random variable X, we have 
    X = F_X^{-1}(U).



Proof. For any x, we have 
    P(X \le x) = F_X(x) = P(U \le F_X(x)) = P(F_X^{-1}(U) \le x).
 Thus X = F_X^{-1}(U).

title: Inverse Sampling Transform
section: 2 Application: Uniform Sampling on a Disk
text:
2 Application: Uniform Sampling on a Disk
Now, we want to perform uniform sampling on the unit disk. We use polar coordinates; more specifically, we take r\cos(\theta), r\sin(\theta), where

r \in [0,1] such that P(r) \propto r (\Rightarrow P(r) = 2r)
\theta \sim U(0,2\pi)

The key lies in 1., that is, how to sample r such that P(r) = 2r. Let X be the random variable such that P(X = r) = 2r. Then, F_X(x) = \int_0^x 2r\,dr = x^2, and thus F_X^{-1}(y) = \sqrt{y}.

2.1 Code
With above in mind, we sample 10000 points on the unit disk, see Figure 1.


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Sample the points
N = 10000
inv_cdf = lambda x: np.sqrt(x)
R = np.vectorize(inv_cdf)(np.random.uniform(0, 1, N))
T = np.random.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, N)
points = [(r * np.cos(t), r * np.sin(t)) for r, t in zip(R, T)]

# 2. Make a scatter plot
x, y = zip(*points)
plt.scatter(x, y, s=1)
plt.xticks([])
plt.yticks([])
ax = plt.gca()
ax.set_aspect('equal')
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['bottom'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['left'].set_visible(False)
plt.show()








Figure 1: Sampling 10000 points uniformly on the unit disk.

title: The violin
text:
Series · 0 Foundations · 1 Violin · 2 Clarinet · 3 Kalimba · 4 Piano · 5 Drum
The string from Part 0, played two ways. Tension and length set the pitch; the bow forces the overtones onto exact whole numbers.

title: The violin
text:
Operator and spectrum
A violin string is the continuum bead chain of Part 0, so its operator is -c^2\partial_x^2 on [0,L] with tied ends. Its eigenfunctions are \sin(n\pi x/L), and the frequencies are 
f_n = \frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \dots

The four strings share one length and differ in T/\mu, tuned to G3, D4, A4 and E5. A finger shortens the vibrating length, and since f \propto 1/L, stopping the string at a fraction s of its length raises the pitch by a factor 1/(1-s). That is why the semitone markers below bunch together toward the bridge.

title: The violin
text:
Play it


  
  
    Bow (hold)Pizzicato (tap)
     Wooden body
    Press and hold a string. Slide left and right to finger it.
  
  
  Left edge is the nut, right edge the bridge. The ticks mark equal-tempered semitones, at fractions 1 − 2−k/12 of the length. The stems are the partials you hear. The body is a linear filter, so switching it off or on changes their heights, never their positions. Its resonances here (about 280, 470, 550 and 2700 Hz) are approximate textbook values.

title: The violin
text:
What the bow does
The bow grips the string and drags it along (stick) until the string’s tension tears it free and it flies back (slip). Helmholtz watched this through a vibration microscope and described the result in 1863: the string becomes two straight segments joined by one sharp corner, and the corner races around a lens-shaped path, once per period. In modal terms that shape is 
u(x,t) = \sum_{n\ge1} \frac{A}{n^2}\,\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\sin(n\omega_1 t).

The motion repeats exactly every period, so its spectrum sits exactly on n f_1, and the force on the bridge falls off like 1/n. A real string is slightly stiff and its own frequencies run a little sharp (Part 4); the stick–slip cycle locks every partial to the period anyway. A pluck, by contrast, lets each mode ring freely at its own frequency and decay.


    
    BowedPlucked at 1/4
    
    Slowed about 500 times. The faint lens is the envelope the corner traces. Stems: partials of the bridge force.

title: The violin
text:
The body
The string barely moves any air. It rocks the bridge, which drives the wooden body, which radiates. Each link is linear, so it can change how loud each partial is but never move one. Toggle the body above while playing: the stems change height and stay put.

title: The clarinet
text:
Series · 0 Foundations · 1 Violin · 2 Clarinet · 3 Kalimba · 4 Piano · 5 Drum
The violin’s operator again, now acting on air pressure in a tube. Only the boundary condition at one end changes, and half the spectrum disappears.

title: The clarinet
text:
Play it



  
  
    Hold to blow
    Register key
    Closed at reed (clarinet)Open both ends (flute)
  
  
  
  
  Tap holes or pick a fingering, then hold the button (or the space bar; keys 1–7 change fingering). The shading inside the bore is the pressure of the sounding mode: dark at a pressure antinode, pale at a node. The first open hole acts as the end of the tube.

title: The clarinet
text:
Deriving the operator

Follow a thin slab of air in a tube of cross-section A. Let \xi(x,t) be how far the air at x has moved along the tube, and p(x,t) the pressure above room pressure.
The slab between x and x+dx has mass \rho A\,dx, and the pressure difference across it is the only force, so Newton’s law reads \rho\,\xi_{tt} = -p_x.
If the slab stretches by the fraction \xi_x, its pressure drops in proportion. Sound compresses air too quickly for heat to flow, so the constant is the adiabatic bulk modulus K = \gamma P_0, and p = -K\,\xi_x.
Differentiate step 2 in x and step 3 twice in t, and eliminate \xi.







TipThe air column’s operator




p_{tt} = c^2 p_{xx}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{K}{\rho} \approx (343\ \text{m/s})^2 .




At an open end the air meets the room, so p = 0. At the reed the opening is nearly shut, so the air cannot move: \xi = 0 there, and by step 2, p_x = 0.

title: The clarinet
text:
Spectrum
The condition p_x(0) = 0 at the reed leaves X = \cos kx, and p(L) = 0 at the open end requires \cos kL = 0. So 
k_n = \frac{(2n-1)\pi}{2L}, \qquad f_n = \frac{(2n-1)\,c}{4L}.

Only odd multiples survive. A flute is open at both ends: p = 0 at both ends gives \sin(n\pi x/L) and f_n = nc/2L, every multiple. Two consequences, both audible above:

An octave lower. The same tube sounds c/4L closed at one end but c/2L open at both. Switch the type and listen.
A twelfth, not an octave. The register key makes the tube jump to its next mode. For the clarinet that is 3f_1, an octave plus a fifth; for the flute it is 2f_1. This is why clarinet fingerings repeat a twelfth apart.

Like the bow, the reed is a valve driven by the pressure it creates, so the oscillation is periodic and its partials sit exactly on n f_1. In the low register the even ones are weak, not zero. A real bore is not perfectly cylindrical and the bell matters; those refine the numbers, not the picture.

title: Foundations: from Newton to an operator
text:
Series · 0 Foundations · 1 Violin · 2 Clarinet · 3 Kalimba · 4 Piano · 5 Drum
Build a string out of beads, apply Newton’s law to one bead, and let the beads crowd together. The wave equation falls out, and so does the reason a string’s overtones are whole numbers.

title: Foundations: from Newton to an operator
text:
One bead, two pulls

Put N beads of mass m on a massless thread with tension T, spaced h apart, with both ends tied down. Let u_j be the height of bead j, and set u_0 = u_{N+1} = 0 for the tied ends.
The thread on the right pulls bead j along itself with force T. For small slopes its vertical part is T\sin\theta \approx T\tan\theta = T(u_{j+1}-u_j)/h. The thread on the left contributes T(u_{j-1}-u_j)/h.
Newton’s second law for bead j is therefore 
m\,\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{h}\left(u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}\right).


The right side is a second difference: it measures how far bead j sits below the average of its neighbors. Drag a bead and watch the arrows.


    
    Beads N5
    ReleaseReset to a pluckHear these beads
    Arrows show the net vertical force on each bead, rescaled to stay visible as N grows. Drag any bead, then release.

title: Foundations: from Newton to an operator
text:
Crowd the beads together

Fix the total length L = (N+1)h and the mass per length \mu = m/h. Dividing the bead equation by m = \mu h gives 
\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{\mu}\cdot\frac{u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}}{h^2}.

As h \to 0 the second difference divided by h^2 tends to u_{xx}, by Taylor’s theorem. With c^2 = T/\mu this is the wave equation.







TipThe string’s operator




u_{tt} = -\mathcal{L}u, \qquad \mathcal{L} = -c^2\partial_x^2, \qquad u(0) = u(L) = 0 .



The bead chain also has an exact spectrum. Its frequencies are \omega_n = 2\sqrt{T/mh}\,\sin\big(n\pi/2(N+1)\big) for n = 1,\dots,N. Slide N up: for small n the sine is nearly linear, and the stems land on the integer grid.


    Spectrum of the bead chain
    
    
    Gray lines are whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency. Stem height is how strongly the current shape excites each mode.
  

The assumptions were small slopes, tension unchanged by stretching, no bending stiffness and no air. Each later instrument relaxes one of them.

title: Foundations: from Newton to an operator
text:
The recipe for every instrument
Each part repeats two moves. The operator is the restoring force per unit mass, written as a function of the shape: tension gives -c^2\partial_x^2, bending gives \kappa^2\partial_x^4, tension in a sheet gives -c^2\Delta. The boundary conditions record what each support forbids.

title: The piano
text:
Series · 0 Foundations · 1 Violin · 2 Clarinet · 3 Kalimba · 4 Piano · 5 Drum
A piano string is a violin string that is also a little bit of a kalimba tine. The two restoring forces add, and the overtones creep sharp.

title: The piano
text:
Play it



  
  Stiffness ×1.0
  Tap a key, or use the computer keys A W S E D F T G Y H U J K for C4 to C5.
  At stiffness 0 every string is ideal and the partials sit on the integers. The default stiffness rises toward the treble, as on a real piano; its size here is illustrative.

title: The piano
text:
Deriving the operator
A piano wire is under heavy tension, like a violin string, and it is thick steel, so it also resists bending, like a kalimba tine. Forces per unit length simply add: the tension term from Part 0 and the bending term from Part 3 give 
\mu\,u_{tt} = T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx}, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad \mathcal{L} = -c^2\partial_x^2 + \kappa^2\partial_x^4 .

Treat the ends as pinned: they cannot move and transmit no bending moment, so u = u_{xx} = 0. Real piano strings are held closer to clamped, which shifts the numbers slightly but not the picture.

title: The piano
text:
Spectrum
Pinned ends make \sin(n\pi x/L) an eigenfunction of both terms at once. Substituting it gives \omega^2 = c^2k^2 + \kappa^2 k^4 with k = n\pi/L, so 
f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}, \qquad B = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{T L^2}.

The stiffness constant B is small, but it multiplies n^2, so high partials run noticeably sharp. Since I grows like the fourth power of the wire’s diameter and B falls like 1/L^2, short thick treble strings are the stiffest.


    Partials of the last key
    
    
    Hammer at 1/8 of the length, so the 8th and 16th partials nearly vanish.

title: The piano
text:
Why tuners stretch octaves
A tuner sets an octave by listening for beats between the lower note’s second partial and the upper note’s fundamental. Stiffness pushes that second partial above 2f_0, so a beat-free octave is slightly wider than 2 : 1. Repeated across the keyboard, this is stretch tuning: the top of a piano is tuned sharp of equal temperament, and the bottom flat.


    C4 + C5, exactly 2 : 1C4 + C5, stretched
    
    Listen for the slow wobble in the 2 : 1 version. Raise the stiffness above to speed it up.

title: The drum
text:
Series · 0 Foundations · 1 Violin · 2 Clarinet · 3 Kalimba · 4 Piano · 5 Drum
The string’s operator in two dimensions. The zeros of Bessel functions replace the whole numbers, and where you strike decides which modes speak.

title: The drum
text:
Play it



  
  Tension ×1.00
  Tap the head anywhere. The ring marks where we listen.
  The motion is the real superposition of the 40 lowest modes, slowed about 300 times. Strike dead center: only round modes appear. Strike on a nodal line of a mode and that mode stays silent.

title: The drum
text:
Deriving the operator

A drumhead is a sheet under tension T, measured as force per unit length of any cut through it, with mass \sigma per unit area. Take a small patch D of it.
Along each piece ds of the patch’s edge, the outside sheet pulls with force T\,ds along the surface. For small slopes its vertical part is T\,\partial_n u\,ds, where \partial_n u is the slope in the outward direction.
Adding these up and applying the divergence theorem gives the net vertical force, 
T\oint_{\partial D} \partial_n u\,ds = T\iint_D \Delta u\,dA .

Newton’s law for the patch is \iint_D \sigma u_{tt}\,dA = T\iint_D \Delta u\,dA. This holds for every patch, so the integrands agree.







TipThe drumhead’s operator




u_{tt} = -\mathcal{L}u,\qquad \mathcal{L} = -c^2\Delta,\qquad c^2 = T/\sigma,\qquad u = 0 \text{ on the rim}.



In one dimension the patch is a segment, its edge is two endpoints, and step 3 is the fundamental theorem of calculus. That is Part 0’s equation again.


    
      
      
      
      
      
      
      patch DT ds
    
    Tension pulls outward all around the edge. Where the sheet bulges, the pulls tilt and their vertical parts add up to T times the Laplacian of u, per unit area.

title: The drum
text:
Spectrum
Separating variables in polar coordinates gives standing waves J_m(kr)\cos m\theta and J_m(kr)\sin m\theta, with J_m a Bessel function; the second solution of Bessel’s equation blows up at the center and is discarded. The rim condition is J_m(ka) = 0, so 
f_{m,n} = \frac{c\,j_{m,n}}{2\pi a},
 where j_{m,n} is the n-th zero of J_m. These zeros are not evenly spaced and no common base frequency fits them, so the drum has no clear pitch. Each frequency with m \ge 1 belongs to two modes, \cos m\theta and \sin m\theta: the round head’s symmetry, visible in the spectrum.
A strike at p, heard at q, gives mode k the weight X_k(p)X_k(q)/\lVert X_k\rVert^2, the eigen-expansion of a point kick. Tap a stem to see one mode on the drumhead and hear it alone.

title: The kalimba
text:
Series · 0 Foundations · 1 Violin · 2 Clarinet · 3 Kalimba · 4 Piano · 5 Drum
Take away the tension and keep only stiffness. A steel tine clamped at one end obeys a fourth-order equation, its overtones scatter far from the integers, and it still sounds pitched.

title: The kalimba
text:
Play it



  
  
     Overtones ring as long as the fundamental
    Tap a tine, or drag across several.
  
  Tine lengths are drawn from the operator: frequency goes as 1/L², so each tine's length is the C4 tine's divided by the square root of its frequency ratio. Tick the box and pluck again to hear the same spectrum as a bell.

title: The kalimba
text:
Deriving the operator

Bend a thin bar. Fibers on the outside of the curve stretch and fibers on the inside compress. By Hooke’s law their stresses add up to a bending moment proportional to the curvature, M = EI\,u_{xx}, where E is Young’s modulus of the steel and I is the second moment of area of the cross-section.
Cut out a slice of length dx. Its two faces carry moments and vertical shear forces. A thin slice has negligible rotational inertia, so its torques balance, which forces the shear to be the slope of the moment: V = -M_x.
Vertical forces do not balance; their difference accelerates the slice. With density \rho and area A, Newton’s law reads \rho A\,u_{tt} = V_x = -M_{xx}. Substituting step 1 gives the operator below.
The clamp forbids moving and tilting: u = u_x = 0 at the base. Nothing grips the tip, so it carries no moment and no shear: u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 there.







TipThe tine’s operator




u_{tt} = -\kappa^2 u_{xxxx}, \qquad \kappa^2 = \frac{EI}{\rho A}.





    
      
      
      
      
      
      
      MM + dM
      VV + dV
      dx
    
    One slice of the tine. Moments (warm) bend it; shear forces (cool) push it up and down. Torque balance links them; force balance moves the slice.

title: The kalimba
text:
Spectrum
A standing wave X(x)\cos\omega t needs X'''' = \beta^4 X with \beta^4 = \omega^2/\kappa^2. The solutions are combinations of \cos\beta x, \sin\beta x, \cosh\beta x and \sinh\beta x. The four boundary conditions are four linear equations for the four coefficients, and they have a nonzero solution exactly when 
\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1 .

The roots are \beta L = 1.8751,\ 4.6941,\ 7.8548,\ 10.9955, \dots, computed live on this page. Since \omega = \kappa\beta^2, the frequency ratios are (\beta_n/\beta_1)^2 = 1 : 6.27 : 17.55 : 34.39. Bending makes frequency grow like the square of the wavenumber, so the overtones fly apart.
The same formula gives f_1 \propto 1/L^2. Kalimba makers tune a tine by sliding it over the bridge to change its free length.
The tine sounds pitched anyway because its first overtone is weak, sits more than two octaves up, and dies within a few hundredths of a second. The ear hears the fundamental with a short metallic click on top.

title: How to Break Nested For Loop
text: Using a few examples, we demonstrate how to conditionally break out of nested for loop using for-else clause.

title: How to Break Nested For Loop
How to Break Nested For Loop
text:
2 Double Nested for Loop
Here, the program halts right after (i,j) reaches (2,1), which is what we want.

for i in range(4): # Layer 1
    print(f"Layer 1 for i = {i}: start")
    for j in range(3): # Layer 2
        print(f"  {i} {j}")
        if (i, j) == (2, 1):
            break
    else: # reached <=> for loop layer 2 was broken
        print(f"  Layer 2 for i = {i}: finished")
        continue # continuing for the enclosing for loop (layer 1), thus ignoring the "break"
    break # reached <=> continue was not called <=> for loop layer 2 was broken

Layer 1 for i = 0: start
  0 0
  0 1
  0 2
  Layer 2 for i = 0: finished
Layer 1 for i = 1: start
  1 0
  1 1
  1 2
  Layer 2 for i = 1: finished
Layer 1 for i = 2: start
  2 0
  2 1


Here, no continue in the else part. Thus, the program breaks unconditionally after finishing its job in the i==0 round.

for i in range(4):
    print(f"Layer 1 for i = {i}: start")
    for j in range(3):
        print(f"  {i} {j}")
        if (i, j) == (2, 1):
            break
    else: # reached <=> the for loop layer 2 was broken
        print(f"  Layer 2 for i = {i}: completed")
    break # always reached at i = 0

Layer 1 for i = 0: start
  0 0
  0 1
  0 2
  Layer 2 for i = 0: completed

title: How to Break Nested For Loop
text:
3 Triple Nested for Loop
OK, we’ve learnt enough. Now, let’s test it on a triple nested for loop!

for i in range(3):
    for j in range(4):
        for k in range(2):
            print(i, j, k)
            if (i,j,k) == (1,2,0):
                break
        else:
            continue
        break
    else:
        continue
    break

title: A Bicycle Wheel
